\"I Finally Don't Have to Ask My Wife to Read the Menu for Me\" — Luke, 62
Vision decline has never been just about \"not seeing clearly.\" Luke used to love taking his wife to breakfast at that little family restaurant in town on weekends. But then, he stopped ordering for himself. Not because the food wasn't good — but because he couldn't read the small print on the menu. Every time the server handed him the menu, he would lean back slightly, squint, pretend to be thinking, and then smile and say: \"Honey, you order for me. I love whatever you pick.\" He would eat the whole meal in silence. Not because of his personality — but because of embarrassment. But what bothered him even more were the \"little things.\" One day, his granddaughter asked him to read the instructions on a medicine bottle. He stared at it for a long time, then finally said: \"The print is too small. Put it on the table and I'll take another look.\" But even on the table, he couldn't see it clearly. He didn't want his granddaughter to think Grandpa was old and useless. At night, driving became harder. He grew more and more afraid of oncoming headlights. Not because his eyes were sensitive to light — but because he lacked confidence in himself. He couldn't see road signs clearly. Couldn't see pedestrians. Couldn't see lane markings. One rainy day, he almost turned down the wrong street. After that, he voluntarily said: \"You drive at night from now on.\" His wife didn't say anything. She just quietly took the keys. He tried many things. He bought three pairs of reading glasses with different strengths — left one pair at home, one in the car, one in his pocket. He tried increasing the font size on his phone to maximum, but still couldn't read the medicine instructions. He even considered surgery, but he was afraid of the risks, the recovery time, and the cost. Then his wife came across BalanceVie online. \"Anyway, we have 30 days to get our money back. Just think of it as trying one more time with me,\" she said. The change came faster than he expected. The first three days — nothing. He thought he had wasted his money again. But on the fifth night, he suddenly noticed that the text on his phone didn't seem as blurry as before. In the second week, he voluntarily picked up a takeout menu from the restaurant — squinted at it for ten seconds, and actually read three menu items out loud. His wife was stunned. Then she smiled. Harder than he had seen her smile in a long time. In the third week, he did something he hadn't dared to do in ages: He drove himself to the supermarket. He made it back home, having read the road signs, the traffic light countdowns, and the parking space lines. He walked in the door, put down the keys, and said: \"I'll drive tomorrow night. Let's go out for dinner.\" He said: BalanceVie isn't selling glasses. \"I've bought a lot of eye care products, but BalanceVie is different.
